property_summary: For any caller address newOwner and when an admin calls setOwner(newOwner), the contract's public owner getter equals the provided newOwner; the mutant instead always sets owner to the stored admin, so for inputs where newOwner != admin the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller addr passed as _owner to setOwner, the reference contract sets owner to that _owner (owner == _owner) after the call; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, breaking this when admin calls setOwner with an _owner different from admin.

For any admin-invoked setOwner(newOwner) call, the contract's public owner getter must equal the supplied newOwner after the call; the mutant that omits assigning owner breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller address supplied to setOwner by the admin, the contract's public owner() should equal the supplied _owner after the call; the mutant violates this by resetting owner to address(0) and thus owner() != _owner for some inputs.

The original contract guarantees that only the deployer (admin) can call setOwner so owner can only be changed when tx.origin/admin is the deployer; the mutant allows the current owner to call setOwner instead, so there exist inputs (caller = owner) where the mutant permits a setOwner call that the reference rejects.

For every call to setOwner by the admin, the reference contract returns true (bool true) while the mutant can return false for some inputs (specifically when previous owner == address(0)), so the returned boolean is always true in the reference but sometimes false in the mutant.

For any caller that is the admin, calling setOwner(x) returns true (the reference always returns true), while the mutant may return false when the prior owner is address(0); the test fuzzes a candidate admin address and a new owner and asserts that an admin call to setOwner returns true.

For any address newOwner and any admin caller, calling setOwner(newOwner) returns true on the reference implementation (it always returns true when called by admin); the mutant can return false when the previous owner is address(0) because it returns (previous != address(0)).

For any admin caller and any new owner address, calling setOwner returns true on the correct contract; the mutant can return false when the prior owner is address(0) — so the property is: an admin call to setOwner always returns true (the reference always returns true), which the mutant violates for some inputs.

For any address newOwner set by the admin, calling setOwner(newOwner) returns a boolean that is equal to true iff the resulting owner is non-zero; the reference always returns true (owner becomes newOwner so non-zero if newOwner!=0) while the mutant can return false when previous owner==address(0) despite owner being set — so we assert that the return value equals (c.owner() != address(0)).

For any caller who is the admin, calling setOwner(addr) always returns true (the reference always returns true on successful calls); the mutant returns false for some valid admin calls, violating that rule.

For all callers, onlyAdmin enforces that setOwner returns true only when called by the admin; the mutant that removes the require lets non-admin callers successfully call setOwner and still return true, violating that admin-restriction observable via the return/behavior for some callers.

For all callers and inputs, only the initial admin (deployer) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant that removes the onlyAdmin check allows non-admin callers to change owner, violating this invariant.

For all callers, only the original admin (the deployer) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant that removes the admin check allows some non-admin caller to change owner, violating this rule.
